summary.text: For \(n=67\), the distinct values \(m=147\) and \(m=2055\) both give the required sum: \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\) and \(1+3+9\cdot7=67\), respectively, from their residues modulo successive powers of two. Thus the multiplicity at \(67\) is at least two, contradicting the claimed uniqueness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be A049802. Thus A383327 is the sequence
\[
a(n)=\#\{m:F(m)=n\}.
\]
In the bounded formulation used to define this count, for nonzero \(n\) one counts the indices \(m<2^{n+1}\) satisfying \(F(m)=n\); this is a sufficient bound for all such indices. For the disproof, it is enough in either formulation to exhibit two distinct indices in that range having value \(67\).

The conjectured set is
\[
S=\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
In particular, \(67\in S\). We will calculate \(F(147)\) and \(F(2055)\).

First consider \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The seven residues occurring in the definition of \(F(147)\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
k&147\bmod 2^k\\ \hline
1&1\\
2&3\\
3&3\\
4&3\\
5&19\\
6&19\\
7&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, modulo \(2\) the odd number \(147\) has residue \(1\); modulo \(4\) it has residue \(3\); modulo \(8\) and \(16\), the difference \(147-3=144\) is divisible by the respective modulus; and modulo \(32,64,128\), the difference \(147-19=128\) is divisible by the respective modulus. Therefore
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]

Next consider \(m=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Write \(2055=2048+7\). Its first three relevant residues are
\[
2055\bmod 2=1,
\qquad
2055\bmod 4=3,
\qquad
2055\bmod 8=7.
\]
For every \(k\) with \(4\le k\le11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2048=2^{11}\), while \(0\le7<2^k\). Hence
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7
\qquad(4\le k\le11).
\]
There are eight integers \(k\) from \(4\) through \(11\). Consequently,
\[
F(2055)=1+3+7+8\cdot7=11+56=67.
\]

The indices \(147\) and \(2055\) are distinct. They also both lie inside the bounded counting range for \(a(67)\), because
\[
147<2055<2^{68}=2^{67+1}.
\]
Thus the set
\[
\{m<2^{68}:F(m)=67\}
\]
contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2055\). Its cardinality is therefore at least two, so
\[
a(67)\ge2,
\]
and in particular \(a(67)\ne1\).

Because \(67\in S\), the conjecture’s universal assertion would require \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts the two explicit occurrences above. Hence it is false that \(a(n)=1\) for every
\(n\in\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}\), which disproves the conjecture.
